abbot: The leader of a monastery. The word comes from "abba", which means "father". The monks promise to obey him.
abolitionists: People who fought to abolish (completely end) slavery. Many of them did it because of their Christian faith.
acts: The Book of Acts (or "Acts of the Apostles") is the fifth book of the New Testament. Luke wrote it to tell the story of the first Christians after Jesus.
acts of the apostles: A book of the New Testament written by Luke. It tells how the first Christians spread the news about Jesus, from Jerusalem all the way to Rome.
adolf hitler: The dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. He started World War II and ordered the murder of six million Jews, a crime called the Holocaust.
aggiornamento: An Italian word meaning "bringing up to date". Pope John XXIII used it to say that the Church should speak in a way that modern people understand.
amazing grace: A very famous Christian song written in 1772 by John Newton, a former slave-ship captain who changed his life. It says: "I once was lost, but now am found."
ambrose: The bishop of Milan (about 340–397). He was so loved that the people chose him as bishop before he was even baptized! He baptized Augustine.
amphitheatre: A big oval stadium with rows of seats, where the Romans watched fights of gladiators and wild animals. The Colosseum in Rome is the most famous one.
anglican: The family of churches that came from the Church of England. It is a bit Catholic (bishops, beautiful ceremonies) and a bit Protestant (no Pope).
antioch: A big, rich city of the Roman Empire, in today's Turkey. It was there that Jesus' followers were first called "Christians".
apostles: From the Greek word for "sent out". The twelve close friends of Jesus whom he sent to tell the world about him. Paul is also called an apostle.
aramaic: The everyday language spoken by Jesus and the people of his region. It is a cousin of Hebrew. A few villages in Syria still speak it today!
aristotle: A very famous Greek philosopher who lived 350 years before Jesus. He wrote about almost everything: logic, nature, animals, politics and happiness.
arius: A priest from Alexandria, in Egypt (about 256–336). He taught that the Son was created by the Father and so was not fully God. The Council of Nicaea said he was wrong.
ascension: When Jesus went up to heaven, 40 days after Easter, according to the Bible. Christians celebrate it on a Thursday in spring.
athanasius: A young deacon, later bishop of Alexandria (about 296–373). He fought all his life for the idea that Jesus is truly God. He was exiled five times!
atlantic slave trade: From the 1500s to the 1800s, about 12 million Africans were captured, taken across the Atlantic Ocean in terrible ships, and sold as slaves in the Americas.
baptism: A ceremony with water that shows someone is joining the Christian family. The water is a sign of being washed clean and starting a new life with God.
barbarians: The name the Romans gave to people living outside their empire who didn't speak Latin or Greek. For the Greeks, their language sounded like "bar-bar-bar"!
baroque: A style of art and buildings from the 1600s. It is full of movement, gold, curves, light and emotion, to amaze people and touch their hearts.
bethlehem: A small town near Jerusalem, where King David was born 1,000 years before Jesus. The prophets said the Messiah would come from there.
bible: The holy book of Christians. It is actually a library of 66 (or 73) books, written over more than 1,000 years, divided into the Old and the New Testament.
byzantine empire: The name historians give to the Eastern Roman Empire, which continued for 1,000 years after Rome fell. Its capital was Constantinople, once called Byzantium.
canaan: The old name of the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, more or less today's Israel and Palestine. The Bible calls it the "Promised Land".
cannons: Big guns that fire heavy balls using gunpowder. They were quite new in 1453, and they could smash walls that had resisted for centuries.
canterbury: A town in the south-east of England. Its archbishop is still the most important bishop of the Church of England and of all Anglicans in the world.
cardinals: Important helpers of the Pope, dressed in red. When a pope dies, the cardinals under 80 years old meet to choose the next one.
carthage: A great city in North Africa, near today's Tunis. It was once Rome's big enemy, then became a rich Roman city with many Christians.
catacombs: Long underground tunnels outside Rome where early Christians buried their dead. The walls have niches for the bodies and beautiful paintings.
cathedrals: The main church of a city, where the bishop has his chair ("cathedra" in Latin). Often the biggest and most beautiful church around.
catholic: From the Greek word for "universal" (for everyone, everywhere). The Catholic Church is the largest Christian church, led by the Pope in Rome.
catholic reformation: The effort of the Catholic Church in the 1500s and 1600s to fix its problems and answer the Protestants. Also called the Counter-Reformation.
census: An official counting of all the people in a country. The Romans did it to know how many taxes they could collect. Countries still do it today.
charismatic: From the Greek word "charisma", meaning "gift". Charismatic Christians pray with a lot of joy and believe in special gifts of the Holy Spirit, like healing.
christmas: The feast of the birth of Jesus, celebrated on the 25th of December (or the 7th of January in many Orthodox churches). "Christ-mass" means the Mass of Christ.
clare: Clare of Assisi (1194–1253), a young noblewoman who ran away from home at 18 to follow Francis. She founded the Poor Clares, nuns who live in poverty and prayer.
concentration camp: A terrible prison camp built by the Nazis, where millions of people, above all Jews, were forced to work, starved and murdered. Auschwitz was the biggest.
conclave: From the Latin "with a key": the cardinals are locked in the Sistine Chapel until they choose a new pope. White smoke from the chimney means: we have a pope!
confessions: A book written by Augustine around 400. It tells the story of his life, his mistakes and how he found God. It is like one long prayer.
confucius: A great Chinese thinker who lived 500 years before Jesus. He taught respect for parents, good manners, kindness and wisdom. His ideas shaped China for 2,000 years.
conquistadors: Spanish word for "conquerors". The Spanish soldiers and explorers who conquered the Americas in the 1500s, like Cortés (Aztecs) and Pizarro (Incas).
constantinople: The city founded by Emperor Constantine in 330 as the new capital of the Roman Empire. Today it is Istanbul, in Turkey.
conversion: Changing your beliefs or your way of life completely, for example becoming a Christian, or turning away from bad things to follow God.
copts: The Christians of Egypt. Their church is one of the oldest in the world: they say it was founded by Mark, the writer of a Gospel. There are about 10 million of them.
council: A big meeting of bishops to take important decisions for the Church. A council of the whole Church is called an "ecumenical" council.
creed: From the Latin "credo", meaning "I believe". A short text that sums up the main things Christians believe.
crucifixion: A very cruel Roman punishment: the person was nailed or tied to a wooden cross and left to die. It was used for slaves and rebels.
cyrillic: The alphabet used today in Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Serbia and other countries. It was named after Saint Cyril, and many of its letters come from Greek.
damascus: A very old city, today the capital of Syria. People have lived there for more than 4,000 years!
demons: In Christian belief, bad spirits, fallen angels who try to lead people away from God. The desert monks told many stories about fighting them.
denominations: The different branches or families of Christianity, like Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Baptist or Pentecostal.
devil: Also called Satan. In the Bible, he is the enemy of God, a fallen angel who tries to tempt people to do bad things.
disciples: Students or followers of a teacher. Jesus had many disciples, and he chose twelve of them to be his closest friends, the apostles.
dnieper: One of the biggest rivers of Europe. It flows through Russia, Belarus and Ukraine, right through the city of Kyiv, into the Black Sea.
dominicans: A group of friars founded by Saint Dominic in 1216. They live simply and dedicate themselves to studying and preaching. They wear white robes.
druids: The priests, teachers and judges of the ancient Celtic peoples, in places like Ireland, Britain and Gaul. They did not write down their teachings.
easter: The most important Christian feast. It celebrates the resurrection of Jesus on a Sunday in spring. Eggs are a symbol of new life!
ecumenical council: A meeting of bishops from the whole Christian world ("ecumenical" means "from the whole inhabited world" in Greek).
ecumenism: The effort to bring Christians of different churches together, so that they understand each other, pray together and one day are united again.
enlightenment: A movement of ideas in the 1700s. Thinkers like Voltaire said people should use reason and science and be free to think for themselves.
epistles: A fancy word for letters. The New Testament contains 21 epistles, 13 of them from Paul, written to churches or to friends.
eternal life: Christians believe that life doesn't end with death: those who are with God will live with him forever, in heaven.
eucharist: From the Greek word for "thank you". The ceremony where Christians share bread and wine to remember the Last Supper. It is also called Mass, Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper.
excommunication: A punishment in which someone is excluded from the Church and can no longer receive communion. It is meant to make them change their mind.
filioque: A Latin word meaning "and from the Son". The West added it to the Creed to say that the Holy Spirit comes from the Father and from the Son. The East did not agree.
florence nightingale: An English nurse (1820–1910) who cared for wounded soldiers at night with her lamp. She made hospitals cleaner and invented modern nursing. She said God had called her.
flying buttresses: Stone arches built outside a Gothic church. They push against the walls to stop them from falling outwards because of the heavy roof.
forbidden city: The huge palace of the emperors of China in Beijing, with almost 1,000 buildings. Ordinary people were not allowed in, which is why it is called "forbidden".
franciscans: The friars who follow Saint Francis of Assisi. They live in poverty, help the poor and preach. They usually wear a brown robe with a rope belt.
franks: A Germanic people who lived along the River Rhine. They conquered Gaul, which later took their name: France!
fresco: From the Italian word for "fresh". A way of painting on wet plaster. When it dries, the painting becomes part of the wall and lasts for centuries.
friars: From the Latin "frater", meaning "brother". Friars are like monks, but instead of staying in a monastery, they go out into towns to preach and help people.
galilee: A green, hilly region in the north of Israel, around a big lake. Jesus grew up there, in Nazareth, and did most of his teaching there.
gandhi: Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948), the leader who helped India become free from British rule without violence. He admired the Sermon on the Mount.
gargoyles: Stone sculptures of monsters or funny creatures on the roofs of churches. They are gutters that spit out rainwater away from the walls.
genesis: The first book of the Bible. Its name means "beginning". It tells the creation of the world, Adam and Eve, Noah's ark and Abraham.
gentiles: The word the Bible uses for people who are not Jewish. Paul was called "the apostle of the Gentiles".
glagolitic: The very first Slavic alphabet, invented by Saint Cyril around 863. Its letters look a bit like little circles, crosses and triangles.
good friday: The Friday before Easter, when Christians remember the day Jesus died on the cross. It is "good" because Christians believe Jesus gave his life to save people.
good samaritan: A story told by Jesus. A man is attacked by robbers. Two religious men pass by without helping, but a man from Samaria, whom Jews disliked, takes care of him.
good shepherd: Jesus called himself "the Good Shepherd", who knows his sheep and even gives his life for them. It was the favourite picture of the early Christians.
gospels: "Gospel" means "good news". The four books of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John that tell the life, teachings, death and resurrection of Jesus.
gothic: A style of building from the Middle Ages, with pointed arches, very high walls, big colourful windows and towers pointing to the sky.
gregorian chant: A calm kind of singing, in Latin, without instruments, where everyone sings the same melody together. It is named after Pope Gregory the Great.
hebrew bible: The holy scriptures of the Jewish people, written mostly in Hebrew. It contains the Law (Torah), the Prophets and other writings, like the Psalms.
helena: The mother of Emperor Constantine (about 250–330). When she was almost 80, she travelled to the Holy Land and had churches built where Jesus lived.
henry iv: King of France from 1589 to 1610, and one of its most loved kings. He wanted every family to be able to have "a chicken in the pot every Sunday".
henry viii: King of England from 1509 to 1547. He is famous for having six wives and for separating the Church of England from the Pope.
heresy: A belief that the Church considers wrong and against its main teachings. In the Middle Ages, it could be punished very harshly.
hermits: People who choose to live alone, far from others, often in the desert, a forest or a cave, to spend their life praying.
herod: Herod the Great, king of Judea under the Romans. He was a great builder but also very cruel and suspicious; he even had members of his own family killed.
holy spirit: For Christians, the Holy Spirit is God present and acting in the world and in people's hearts. He is often shown as a dove or as flames of fire.
hospitallers: Knight-monks who ran a big hospital in Jerusalem for sick pilgrims, and also protected them with weapons. Today they still exist as the Order of Malta, helping the sick.
huguenots: The name given to French Protestants who followed John Calvin's ideas. They were often persecuted in France.
hundred years' war: A long series of wars between England and France, from 1337 to 1453 (actually 116 years!), to decide who should be king of France.
icons: Holy pictures painted on wood, showing Jesus, Mary or the saints, often on a golden background. Orthodox Christians say icons are "written", not painted!
illuminated manuscripts: Books written by hand and decorated with bright colours, gold and silver, which make the pages "light up" ("illuminate").
inculturation: Expressing the Christian faith using the language, clothes, music and customs of a local culture, instead of copying European ways.
indulgences: In the Catholic Church, a pardon that reduces the punishment for sins after death. In Luther's time, people could buy them with money, which caused a scandal.
industrial revolution: The time, from around 1760 to 1900, when machines, factories, steam engines and railways changed the way people lived and worked.
islam: A religion founded in Arabia in the 600s by the prophet Muhammad. Muslims believe in one God (Allah in Arabic) and their holy book is the Quran.
jerusalem: The holy city of the Jews, where the Temple stood. Jesus died and rose there. It is also holy for Christians and Muslims.
jesuits: Members of the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola in 1540. They are famous for their schools, their missionaries and their scientists. Pope Francis was a Jesuit.
john xxiii: Pope from 1958 to 1963, nicknamed "the Good Pope". He was a peasant's son, full of humour, and started the Second Vatican Council.
justification by faith: Luther's big idea: people are made right with God ("justified") not because of their good actions, but because they trust (have faith in) Jesus.
justinian: Emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire from 527 to 565. He rebuilt Hagia Sophia, reconquered Italy and wrote a big book of laws.
kievan rus': A great medieval state in Eastern Europe, with its capital in Kyiv. Today's Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all consider it as their ancestor.
knights templar: Knight-monks founded in 1119 to protect pilgrims going to Jerusalem. They became very rich and powerful, until the King of France destroyed their order in 1312.
kolkata: A huge city in eastern India, formerly called Calcutta. More than 15 million people live in its area.
latin: The language of the ancient Romans. For centuries it was the language of the Catholic Church, of schools and of scholars. French, Spanish and Italian come from it.
leprosy: A disease that damages the skin and nerves. For centuries, people were terrified of it, and lepers had to live apart from everyone. Today it can be cured.
lord's prayer: The prayer Jesus taught his disciples, starting "Our Father, who art in heaven...". It is the prayer shared by all Christians.
magi: Wise men from the East, probably astrologers from Persia (today's Iran). Tradition later called them the Three Kings: Caspar, Melchior and Balthazar.
manger: A box or trough that holds food (hay) for animals such as cows and donkeys.
martyr: From the Greek word for "witness". Someone who is killed because they refuse to give up their faith.
mary magdalene: A woman from the town of Magdala who followed Jesus. She was the first to see him after his resurrection, so she is called "the apostle to the apostles".
messiah: A Hebrew word meaning "anointed one" (someone marked with holy oil, like a king). The Jews waited for a Messiah sent by God. In Greek, it is "Christ".
middle ages: The period of European history between the Roman Empire and the Renaissance, roughly from the year 500 to 1500. The time of castles, knights and cathedrals.
ministry: Here, it means the time when Jesus was travelling, teaching and healing people, about three years before his death.
miracles: Amazing events that cannot be explained by the ordinary laws of nature, which believers see as signs of God's power.
missionaries: People sent to other places or countries to spread their religion, and often to open schools and hospitals.
missionary journeys: Long trips made to spread the Christian message. Paul made three big ones, and a last one as a prisoner to Rome.
monastery: A place where monks or nuns live together, pray, work and study. A monastery for women is sometimes called a convent.
monks: Men who give their whole life to God. They live in a monastery, don't marry, own nothing personally and pray many times a day.
monte cassino: A monastery on top of a mountain in Italy, founded by Saint Benedict. It was destroyed many times, the last time in World War II, and always rebuilt.
mosaics: Pictures made by sticking together thousands of tiny coloured pieces of stone or glass, sometimes covered with gold.
moses: The great leader of the Hebrews in the Bible. He led them out of slavery in Egypt, through the Red Sea, and received the Ten Commandments from God.
mosque: A building where Muslims pray together, especially on Fridays. It often has a dome and tall towers called minarets.
movable type: Little metal blocks, each with one letter, that can be arranged to print a page, then taken apart and reused for the next page.
nazi: The party led by Adolf Hitler in Germany. The Nazis believed some races were superior to others and committed terrible crimes during World War II.
nero: Roman emperor from 54 to 68. He was known for his cruelty: he even had his own mother killed. He was the first emperor to persecute Christians.
new testament: The second part of the Christian Bible, with 27 books written after Jesus: the four Gospels, the Acts, the letters and the Book of Revelation.
nicaea: An ancient city in today's Turkey (now called İznik), where the first great council of the Church took place in 325.
nicene creed: The statement of Christian belief written by the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). Most Christian churches still recite it.
nobel peace prize: A famous prize given every year to a person or group that has worked hard for peace in the world. It was created by Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite.
nonviolence: Fighting injustice without using violence: with marches, boycotts, refusing to obey unfair laws, and love, even towards your enemies.
notre-dame de paris: The famous Gothic cathedral on an island in the middle of Paris. Its name means "Our Lady", which is a name for Mary, the mother of Jesus.
nuns: Women who give their whole life to God, living together in a community, praying and often teaching, nursing or helping the poor.
old testament: The first part of the Christian Bible. It contains the Jewish scriptures written before Jesus: the creation, Abraham, Moses, the kings and the prophets.
olympic games: Sports games held every four years in Olympia, Greece, in honour of the god Zeus, from 776 BC. They were restarted in modern times in 1896.
ora et labora: Latin for "pray and work". It sums up the life of Benedictine monks: a balance between prayer and manual work.
orthodox: From the Greek for "right belief" or "right praise". The Orthodox churches are the churches of the East, like the Greek, Russian or Serbian Church.
ottoman empire: A powerful Turkish Muslim empire founded around 1300. It lasted more than 600 years, until 1922, and ruled a big part of the Middle East, North Africa and South-East Europe.
pagans: The word Christians used for people who worshipped the old gods, like Jupiter, Odin or Perun. It comes from the Latin for "country people".
palm sunday: The Sunday before Easter, when Christians remember Jesus entering Jerusalem as people waved palm branches. Churches often hand out palm or olive branches.
parables: Short stories with a hidden lesson that Jesus used to teach people about God, using everyday things like seeds, sheep, coins and bread.
parchment: A writing material made from the skin of sheep, goats or calves, cleaned, stretched and dried. It lasts much longer than paper.
passover: A big Jewish festival in spring. It celebrates the time God freed the Hebrews from slavery in Egypt, with a special meal.
patriarch: The title of the leader of an important Orthodox church, like the Patriarch of Constantinople or of Moscow. It means "father-leader".
patron saint: A saint who is believed to protect a country, a city, a job or a group of people in a special way.
paul vi: Pope from 1963 to 1978. He finished the Second Vatican Council and was the first pope to travel by plane to all five continents.
peace of westphalia: The peace treaties signed in 1648 in two German towns, Münster and Osnabrück. They ended the Thirty Years' War.
penance: Doing something to show you are truly sorry for something wrong you did, and asking God for forgiveness.
pentecost: A Jewish harvest festival 50 days after Passover. For Christians, it is the day the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles.
pentecostal: Christians who give a very big importance to the Holy Spirit, like on the day of Pentecost, with joyful worship, healing prayers and speaking in tongues.
persecution: Hurting, arresting or killing people again and again because of who they are or what they believe.
peter: Simon, a fisherman whom Jesus renamed Peter, meaning "rock". He was the leader of the apostles. Catholics consider him the first Pope.
pharisee: A member of a Jewish group who studied the Law of Moses carefully and tried to obey every little rule of it.
pilgrims: People who travel to a holy place for religious reasons. The Mayflower Pilgrims were travelling to a new land to live their faith freely.
pontius pilate: The Roman governor of Judea from about 26 to 36. He had the power to put people to death. In the Gospels, he "washes his hands" of Jesus' fate.
pope: The bishop of Rome and leader of the Catholic Church. Catholics see him as the successor of Saint Peter. The word comes from "papa", meaning father.
pope francis: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, from Buenos Aires in Argentina. He was pope from 2013 to 2025 and was known for his simple life and his love for the poor.
presbyterian: Churches led not by bishops but by "elders" ("presbyteros" in Greek) chosen by the members. Very common in Scotland, Korea and the USA.
printing press: A machine that presses paper on inked letters to print many copies of the same page quickly. It changed the world!
promise: In the Bible, a promise God makes is also called a "covenant": an agreement between God and his people, like a very special contract.
prophet: A person who speaks for God, gives his messages to people, warns them when they do wrong and gives them hope. Famous prophets include Isaiah, Jeremiah and Elijah.
protestant: The Christians who came out of the Reformation and don't follow the Pope. The name comes from the protest of some German princes in 1529.
purgatory: In Catholic belief, a state after death where souls are purified before entering heaven.
puritans: English Protestants of the 1500s and 1600s who wanted to "purify" the Church of England of everything that looked Catholic. They lived very strict lives.
quakers: A Christian group founded in England in the 1600s. They have no priests, pray in silence together and refuse all violence and war.
red cross: An organization that helps wounded people in wars and disasters, without taking sides. In Muslim countries, it is called the Red Crescent.
reformation: The big movement in the 1500s that wanted to reform (correct) the Church, and led to the birth of the Protestant churches.
reformed: The Protestant churches that follow the ideas of John Calvin and other Swiss reformers.
renaissance: French for "rebirth". A period, from about 1400 to 1600, when art, science and learning flourished in Europe, inspired by ancient Greece and Rome.
resurrection: Coming back to life after death. Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead on the third day, with a new, living body.
revelation: The last book of the Bible, written by a man named John. It is full of mysterious visions about the end of time and God's final victory over evil.
revival: A time when many people suddenly become very interested in faith again, with big, emotional meetings and many conversions.
righteous among the nations: An honour given by Israel to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust. More than 28,000 people have received it.
roman empire: A huge empire that, at the time of Jesus, went all around the Mediterranean Sea, from Spain to Syria, and from England to Egypt. Its capital was Rome.
rome: The capital of the Roman Empire, and today of Italy. Inside Rome is a tiny country, the Vatican, where the Pope lives.
sabbath: The Jewish day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday evening. It remembers that God rested on the seventh day of creation.
sacraments: Holy rituals that Christians see as signs of God's love and grace, like baptism and communion. Catholics and Orthodox count seven of them.
sacrifice: Here, an offering to the gods, like burning incense or an animal on an altar. For Christians, doing this for the Roman gods meant giving up their faith.
saint: A person who lived a very holy life, close to God. Churches honour them as examples to follow.
saint bartholomew's day massacre: A terrible killing of Protestants by Catholics, which started in Paris on the night of the 24th of August 1572 and spread through France.
saint patrick's day: The feast of Saint Patrick on the 17th of March. It is the national holiday of Ireland, and people everywhere wear green and hold parades.
saint peter's basilica: The huge church in the Vatican, built over the tomb of Saint Peter. It was rebuilt in the 1500s and 1600s by artists like Michelangelo.
saints: People who lived very holy lives, close to God. Churches honour them as examples to follow.
sari: A long piece of cloth, about 5 to 9 metres long, that Indian women wrap around their body as a dress.
scaffolding: A temporary structure of wooden planks or metal poles that allows workers to reach high places.
scriptorium: Latin for "a place for writing". The room in a monastery where monks copied and decorated books by hand, in silence.
segregation: Keeping people apart because of their skin colour or origin, with separate schools, buses and restaurants. It was the law in the southern USA until 1964.
seminaries: Special schools where young men study for several years to become priests.
shamrock: A small green plant with three leaves, like clover. It is the symbol of Ireland.
siege: When an army surrounds a city or castle and stops anyone or anything from getting in or out, to force it to surrender.
slavs: A big family of peoples in Central and Eastern Europe who speak related languages: Russians, Ukrainians, Poles, Czechs, Slovaks, Serbs, Croats, Bulgarians and others.
society of jesus: The official name of the Jesuits, the religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola in 1540.
speaking in tongues: Praying aloud with sounds or in a language the person doesn't know. Pentecostals believe it is a gift of the Holy Spirit, as on the day of Pentecost.
spirituals: Songs created by enslaved Africans in America, mixing Bible stories with African rhythms, like "Go Down Moses" and "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot". Some had secret messages about escaping!
stained glass: Pieces of coloured glass held together with strips of lead to make pictures in windows. When the sun shines, the church fills with colours.
sunday schools: Schools held on Sunday, the only free day for working children, to teach them to read and write using the Bible. They began in England in the 1780s.
tacitus: A Roman historian (about 56–120). He wrote about Nero's persecution of the Christians. It is one of the oldest texts outside the Bible that mentions Jesus.
temple: The great Temple in Jerusalem, the holiest place for the Jews, where people came to pray and offer sacrifices to God.
ten commandments: Ten rules given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai, according to the Bible, like "You shall not kill" and "You shall not steal".
thanksgiving: A holiday in the United States (the 4th Thursday of November) and in Canada, when families gather for a big meal to thank God for the harvest and blessings.
theology: From the Greek words for "God" and "study". Thinking carefully about God, the Bible and faith.
thirty years' war: A terrible war in Germany and Central Europe from 1618 to 1648. It started between Catholics and Protestants, then involved almost all the powers of Europe.
thomas more: An English lawyer, writer and politician (1478–1535). He wrote a famous book called "Utopia" about a perfect island. The Catholic Church made him a saint.
tolerance: Accepting that other people can have different beliefs or opinions than yours, and letting them live in peace.
trent: A town in the mountains of northern Italy, called Trento in Italian. It was chosen for the council because it was between Italy and Germany.
trinity: The Christian belief that there is only one God, who is at the same time three persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus) and the Holy Spirit.
underground railroad: Not a real railway! It was a secret network of people and hiding places that helped slaves escape from the South to the free North and Canada.
universities: From the Latin "universitas", meaning a community. Schools for older students, where they could study the highest subjects and get diplomas.
vaults: Arched ceilings made of stone. Rib vaults have stone "ribs" that cross each other and carry the weight, a bit like an umbrella.
visigoths: A Germanic people who sacked the city of Rome in 410. It was the first time in 800 years that an enemy had entered Rome. They later settled in Spain.
vulgate: The Latin translation of the Bible made by Saint Jerome around 400. It was the official Bible of the Catholic Church for centuries.
wars of religion: Wars fought between Catholics and Protestants in Europe in the 1500s and 1600s, especially in France and Germany.
western wall: The last remaining part of the wall around the Temple courtyard in Jerusalem. Jews pray there and slip little prayer notes into the cracks between the stones.
william tyndale: An English scholar (about 1494–1536) who translated the Bible from Hebrew and Greek into English. He was executed for it, but his words live on in the English Bible.
